data.title: India's markets regulator proposes removing additional disclosure requirements for offshore funds
data.description:
India's markets regulator on Friday proposed scrapping additional disclosure requirements for offshore funds, saying beneficial ownership disclosures already provided adequate transparency.

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) currently requires additional disclosures from offshore funds considered high risk — rules that were introduced during its scrutiny of Adani offshore funds in 2023.

These rules require the full disclosure of ultimate owners in offshore funds that have concentrated investments in Indian companies.

SEBI said the requirements were "not in line with globally accepted practices" and "could potentially place India at a competitive disadvantage vis-à-vis peer jurisdictions with relatively lenient regulatory requirements."

Reuters had in August reported SEBI was planning to relax the disclosure requirements, after they led to foreign investor complaints and appeals citing onerous requirements, prompting a review.

data.title: Angola to pay $180 million for 10% of De Beers, Endiama CEO says
data.description:
Angola will pay about $180 million for a 10% stake in De Beers, state diamond miner Endiama's CEO José Manuel Augusto Ganga Júnior said on Friday.

  • Anglo American put De Beers up for sale in 2024 as part of a broader restructuring, as falling diamond prices and rising competition from synthetic stones weighed on the miner's diamond business

  • Angola and neighbouring Namibia will join Botswana, already a 15% shareholder in De Beers, among the diamond giant's new owners, Botswana's President Duma Boko announced on November 9

  • Ganga Júnior said Angola's acquisition of a stake in De Beers, which is exploring for diamonds in the country, still made sense despite a slump in gem prices

  • He was speaking after Endiama commissioned Angola's first gold refinery in Luanda, which has the capacity to process 25 kg per day

data.title: Westlake to pay $199M to settle PVC pipe antitrust claims
data.description:
Westlake disclosed Friday it agreed to pay $199M to settle claims with two remaining plaintiff classes in U.S. PVC pipe price-fixing antitrust litigation, subject to court approval.

The chemical and building products company said it agreed to pay $119.5M to non-converter seller purchasers and $79.5M to end-user class plaintiffs related to the litigation.

Westlake and other PVC pipe and fittings companies were defendants in several class action lawsuits in 2024-25 alleging they conspired with each other and price reporting service OPIS to artificially inflate U.S. prices.

The latest settlement adds to a previously approved $67M settlement with direct purchasers.

The company said it expects to record a pre-tax charge for substantially all the settlement amounts during Q4.

data.title: Robusta coffee hits 3-year low as Vietnam harvest ramps up
data.description:
Robusta coffee futures on the ICE exchange hit three-year lows on Friday, heading for 10% weekly falls as the harvest in top grower Vietnam ramps up.

Raw sugar also hit three-month lows.

COFFEE

* Robusta coffee fell 3.3% to $2,879 a metric ton at 1313 GMT, after setting a three-year low of $2,854.

* A Vietnam-based dealer noted that ICE futures have fallen sharply yet local price discounts for physical robusta are still easing. "That is the clearest sign so far of growing supply pressure," he said.

* Elsewhere, the recent weakness of Brazil's real currency has encouraged exports from the world's second largest robusta producer.

* Brazil's currency fell to its lowest level since April 2025 on Thursday.

* Arabica coffee fell 2% to $2.7080 per lb.

SUGAR

* Raw sugar fell 1.5% to 19.92 cents per lb after setting a three-month low of 16.90.

* Funds have been scaling back a net long position in raw sugar ahead of the year end, with the market looking technically bearish after breaking below key support levels.

* Physical sugar broker Deepcore noted some bearish fundamental factors also, namely, estimates of 13% growth in top grower Brazil's 2027 sugar output and limited interest in India's duty-free raw sugar import programme.

* White sugar lost 0.8% to $484.40 a metric ton.

COCOA

* London cocoa ​​rose 0.8% to £4,067 per ton.

* Low port arrivals in top grower Ivory Coast are helping underpin cocoa, as are estimate for sharply reduced 2026/27 output in Ecuador.

* Ample availability of cocoa from the 2025/26 crop, however, continued to keep a lid on prices.

* New York cocoa gained 0.6% to $5,234 a ton.

data.title: Euro Falls Amid Risk-Off Mood
data.description:
OTTAWA (dpa-AFX) - The euro weakened against other major currencies in the European session on Friday, as European stocks traded lower due to ongoing sell-off in artificial intelligence and chip stocks.

Anthropic's record listing in New York failed to stem concerns over slower AI infrastructure spending and rising debt loads in the sector.

Eurozone consumer confidence figures, final U.S. consumer sentiment data and comments from Fed and ECB officials will be in the spotlight as the day progresses.

In the European trading today, the euro fell to a 1-1/2-month low of 174.01 against the yen and a 3-day low of 0.9219 against the Swiss franc, from early highs of 173.35 and 0.9263, respectively. If the euro extends its downtrend, it is likely to find support around 171.00 against the yen and 0.91 against the franc.

Against the U.S. dollar and the pound, the euro slipped to 1.0957 and 0.8361 from early highs of 1.0990 and 0.8385, respectively. The euro may test support near 1.08 against the greenback and 0.82 against the pound.

The euro slipped to a 2-day low of 1.5695 against the Canadian dollar, from an early high of 1.5739. On the downside, 1.55 is seen as the next support level for the euro.

Looking ahead, Canada retail sales for September, manufacturing and wholesale sales reports for October, U.S. University of Michigan's consumer sentiment for November and U.S. Baker Hughes oil rig count data are slated for release in the New York session.

data.title: BJ's Wholesale Lifts Outlook, Posts Higher 3Q Profit Despite Margin Pressure — Update
data.description:
By Connor Hart

BJ's Wholesale Club raised its full-year outlook after posting higher profit and sales in the recent quarter, though its shares fell as increased promotions weighed on margins.

The warehouse club chain on Friday said it now expects adjusted earnings of $5.10 to $5.30 a share, up from a prior outlook of $4.60 to $4.80 a share.

The company also raised the low end of its forecast for comparable-club sales excluding gasoline to up 2.5% from up 2%, while maintaining the high end at up 3%.

Analysts are looking for adjusted earnings of $4.74 a share and comparable-club sales growth of 2.6%, according to FactSet.

The higher outlook came as BJ's reported what William Blair analysts called largely better-than-expected third-quarter results.

Profit and revenue climbed, boosted by accelerating same-store sales growth. Merchandise margin declined by 170 basis points year-over-year, though, driven by increased promotions.

Shares, however, fell 7%, to $103.05, in premarket trading.

Comparable-club sales, which account for store openings and closings, increased by 4.1% excluding gasoline sales. Analysts were looking for a 2.7% gain.

Total revenues jumped 17% to $6.28 billion, topping Wall Street models for $5.97 billion.

BJ's reported a profit of $219.5 million, or $1.73 a share, for its quarter ended Oct. 31, compared with $152.1 million, or $1.15 a share, a year earlier.

On an adjusted basis, earnings were still $1.73 a share. Analysts had expected adjusted earnings of $1.26 a share.

data.title: Analyst Voices Concerns Over Anthropic's Revenue Growth — Market Talk
data.description: Anthropic will need to see much higher revenue growth rates over the next two years to justify its valuation, Seaport Research Partners analyst Jay Goldberg says in a note. He voices concerns over how Anthropic's growth slowed sharply in 3Q, which he says may not improve much in 4Q. "Anthropic is an incredible company, but it is also asking for an incredible leap of faith by investors," Goldberg says. "We think the company will need time to grow into its valuation and answer some very big questions about its growth trajectory," he says. Goldberg says he's not negative about the stock but merely cautious, assigning a neutral rating to shares.(kelly.cloonan@wsj.com)

data.title: Why China is unwilling to be the world's next climate leader
data.description:
Key points:
  • China has decided against hosting the 2028 COP, sources say
  • Little appetite in Beijing to champion global climate diplomacy
  • Delegation at COP has played its traditional low-profile role

By Lewis Jackson

President Xi Jinping showcased China's diplomatic heft this week at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.

But 5,000 miles away at the COP31 international climate conference in the Turkish city of Antalya, Beijing is sending a different message: we're not the leaders you're looking for.

The exit of the United States from international climate diplomacy under President Donald Trump since last year has left a superpower-sized hole in the COP process that many had hoped China would fill, especially after reports last year it was considering hosting COP33 in 2028.

But Beijing has decided against hosting the annual UN climate conference, two people familiar with the matter said this week. Meanwhile China's envoys to COP31 stuck to the country's accustomed low-key playbook, diplomats and observers to the talks said.

"Yes, we would like to see China take more of a role, simply because right now China is the defender of the international world order and the rule of law in the absence of the previous defenders," said Ralph Regenvanu, Vanuatu's climate minister.

China's delegation has been mostly absent from public events at the two-week conference on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, which is attempting to address rising temperatures and the worsening impacts of climate change.

CHINA SIDES WITH THE DEVELOPING WORLD

Inside the closed-door negotiations, China's delegation fulfilled its traditional role of siding with the developing world's demands that wealthy nations give more climate finance and cut emissions faster, while resisting specific targets for phasing out fossil fuels, diplomats said.

While historically, the Western world has emitted the most greenhouse gases, China is now by far the planet's biggest emitter.

It is also a major part of the solution as the largest producer and exporter of the solar panels, wind turbines and electric vehicles needed to curb carbon emissions.

A Reuters analysis published ahead of the COP31 conference showed that China sent $132 billion in clean technology and investment to the developing world last year, almost on par with all developed world climate finance.

ANOTHER KIND OF LEADERSHIP

The reluctance to leverage those green credentials into a bigger role in international climate diplomacy reflects the prevailing view in Beijing that doing so would have unwelcome consequences, say observers and analysts.

For one, hosting a COP, short for Conference of the Parties, would create pressure for China to propose more ambitious climate targets, which is opposed by groups tied to the country's huge coal sector.

A bigger role on the global climate stage could also spur demands for more climate giving and reopen a long-standing debate over whether the world's second-largest economy belongs in the same league as poorer developing countries.

A person familiar with the Chinese government's thinking said the central government saw no advantage in taking on more formal climate leadership.

"The central government thinks we are already leading on renewable technology, why should we have this COP?" the person said.

China's ministry of foreign affairs did not immediately respond to questions from Reuters.

LINKING TRADE TO CLIMATE

There is one area where Beijing has been willing to take a bigger role: trade.

Just as Xi denounced "rampant protectionism" at the APEC summit this week, Chinese negotiators in Antalya pressed for language on the free flow of green trade as a way to promote the clean-technology industries that have become a major source of economic and geopolitical influence.

That could counter what China sees as trade restrictions the West has imposed only in the name of climate policy.

One European diplomat described the issue as China's key ask in talks with the European Union.

The United States has all but blocked imports of Chinese electric cars with tariffs, while the European Union has also raised barriers to Chinese clean technology and implemented rules designed to tax carbon-heavy imports.

At a pre-COP briefing in Beijing, Li Gao, China's delegation head, told reporters the conference needed to address the "new problem" of unilateralism and protectionism, a common indirect criticism from China of US and European trade policy.
